# How to Turn Spoken Arabic into Written Text with AI (Step-by-Step)

Imagine you've just finished a long phone call with family in Arabic, and you want to remember the funny story your cousin told. Instead of scrambling for a pen, you could speak into your phone and have a clean, written version ready seconds later. That's what modern AI transcription tools can do for Arabic speakers — and you don't need to be a computer expert to use them.

## What "AI transcription" actually means

Transcription is simply turning spoken words into written text. AI transcription uses a computer model — a program trained on thousands of hours of Arabic speech — to listen to an audio file and type out what it hears.

Arabic has its own quirks. Different dialects (think Egyptian, Levantine, Gulf, or Maghrebi) sound quite different from each other, and everyday speech often mixes Arabic with English or French words. Good Arabic transcription tools are trained to handle that mix.

## A real example: transcribing a voice note from start to finish

Let's walk through the whole process using a tool called **Cohere Transcribe Arabic**. It's an AI transcription service built specifically for Arabic speech, and you can try it without installing anything.

**Step 1 — Open the tool in your browser.** Go to Cohere's website and look for the Transcribe Arabic feature on their dashboard. You'll usually find it listed under speech or audio tools. Sign in with a free account if you don't have one yet.

**Step 2 — Pick your dialect.** When you start a new transcription job, the tool will ask which Arabic dialect you're speaking. Choose the closest match — Egyptian, Levantine, Gulf, Maghrebi, or Modern Standard Arabic (the formal version used in news and books). Picking the right dialect makes a big difference to accuracy.

**Step 3 — Upload your audio.** You can either record a short voice note directly in your browser, or upload an audio file you've already saved on your phone or laptop. A 30-second to 2-minute clip is perfect for a first try.

**Step 4 — Let the AI do its work.** Hit the transcribe button and wait a few seconds. The model listens to your audio and writes down what it hears, in real Arabic script, not just Roman letters.

**Step 5 — Read, copy, and save.** Once it's done, you'll see your transcript on screen. From here you can copy the text into a message, a notes app, or a Word document. Some versions let you download it as a plain text or PDF file.

That's the whole flow — about three minutes from audio to written words.

## Where this fits in your day

- **Family voice notes** — Record a message in Arabic on WhatsApp or your phone, then transcribe it so relatives who prefer reading can follow along.
- **Study and revision** — Record a tutorial, then search through the written version later when exam time comes.
- **Brainstorming in Arabic** — Talk through your ideas out loud, and let the AI turn them into a tidy first draft you can edit.
- **Interviews and quotes** — Capture what someone said accurately, without typing while they're still talking.

## What to check before you start

When you're comparing tools (or deciding whether to stick with one), keep these in mind:

- **Dialect support** — Does it cover your specific dialect, or only Modern Standard Arabic?
- **Privacy** — Where does your audio go? Some tools process it on your own device, others send it to a server. For sensitive conversations, that matters.
- **Price** — Many services offer a free tier with a few minutes of audio per month, which is plenty for a first test.
- **Export options** — Can you save the text as a simple document, or does it stay locked inside the app?

Tool features and pricing change often, so it's worth checking the official page directly for the latest details before you commit.

## What this means for you

- **If you speak Arabic at home**: You can finally have those voice notes searchable and readable. No more replaying a three-minute message to find the one address someone mentioned.
- **If you're learning Arabic**: Recording yourself speaking and reading the transcript back is a powerful way to catch pronunciation slips and build vocabulary.
- **If you work with Arabic-speaking clients or communities**: Transcripts make meetings, focus groups, and customer calls much easier to share with colleagues who don't speak Arabic.
- **If you're just curious**: Start with a free account on Cohere Transcribe Arabic, record a 30-second voice note in your own dialect, and see how the transcript compares to what you actually said.

## Wrap-up

AI transcription for Arabic has quietly become good enough for everyday use — no technical background required. The easiest way to start is to pick a tool with a free tier, follow the five steps above with a short voice note, and see how the result looks. Once you see it work once, you'll find dozens of small ways to use it in your week. Your first step today: open Cohere's site, sign up, and try transcribing one voice note in your own dialect.
